fullText:
Critics decry proposed hyperscale projects, fearing overuse of water and electricity, and ‘appropriating rural, Black-owned land for industrial purposes’

There seems to be a fight over datacenters in nearly every city in the US right now. And amid the extreme polarization of today’s politics, the opposition tends to be bipartisan.

“I would say it’s kind of the far left and the far right ran into each other and had a hug,” said Frank Scott Jr, mayor of Little Rock, Arkansas. “But they come at it from different perspectives.”

Two hyperscale datacenter proposals emerged in January in and near Little Rock. Google plans to develop a 1.43m-sq-ft, $1bn datacenter at the Port of Little Rock, on a 384-acre site. The other, by Avaio, is a $6bn project 10 miles south, in a rural patch of marshy forest in unincorporated Pulaski county.

In most places, if enough people show up to city council meetings or county commission hearings, public pressure can kill a project. But Arkansas is uniquely restrained.

Three years ago, lawmakers in Arkansas’ Republican-dominated legislature passed legislation that blocked local ordinances from banning datacenters.

The language in the law is almost an accident, according to state representative David Whitaker, a Democrat from Washington county, Arkansas. “It had nothing to do with datacenters, per se,” he said. “It came in with a big concern of crypto mining in some of our rural areas… They’d buy shipping containers and drop them off in the middle of the night out in a soybean field.”

The term “datacenters” was tacked on in the definitions during the sausage-making process of legislation, somehow. “Nobody was talking about these datacenters in 2023,” said Whitaker.

But Scott, who said he was at the Arkansas state capitol while the bill was being argued, suggested its inclusion “seems very intentional to those involved” now. While state law prohibits communities from outright bans on datacenters, city or county governments have broad authority to regulate them.

The mayor of Little Rock – up for re-election this year – has tried to push back against the proposed projects.

“I think it has a lot to do with water and electricity rates,” Scott said. “Water is, as we know, a security issue. It’s a way of life issue. Then the electricity rates with gas …

“People are very concerned about the dollars, and that this gives not only that, they feel like the datacenters will not pay their fair share. They’re going to use up all the water. They’re going to increase all the electricity, and it’s going to hit their back pocket like gas is right now.”

Arkansas’s nickname is the Natural state, he noted. “So very many people are concerned about our natural resources.”

The datacenter business found in Little Rock the same attributes that crypto miners found to be attractive in Arkansas: cheap land with cheap power. Arkansas industrial electricity customers pay between 5 and 7 cents per kWh, well below the national average of 8.71 cents per kWh, according to the latest figures from the US Energy Information Administration.

Such is the story across the south and midwest. An analysis of planned datacenter projects by Pew Research found three-quarters of all planned datacenters will be built in these two regions, with the south alone accounting for nearly half of them.

Little Rock, Arkansas’s capital city, is second only to Nashville in GDP growth, according to Scott, who has pitched it as a refuge from the crushing cost-of-living increases that are driving people from the coasts. Little Rock is a healthcare and logistics hub with strong job growth. Parts of the city are gentrifying, including the neighborhood around its renowned Central high school.

There are back yards that might want a new datacenter in Arkansas. Those back yards are not in Little Rock, Scott said.

“You have West Memphis, which is a smaller city; they love it,” Scott said, referring to a Google project in Arkansas, just across the border from Tennessee. “Google’s giving $25m for workforce development and impact funds, and so it gives a great example. But I’ve also seen in the news where there are other small cities, the size of West Memphis, who don’t want it and are just as mad as folks here in Little Rock.”

Google was approached for comment.

People in Wrightsville, 10 miles south of Little Rock where the Avaio datacenter project is slated, are hopping mad, too. Unlike the city, the county has reacted less vigorously.

The rural street connecting Wrightsville to I-530 and Little Rock is getting repaved, right around the spot where Avaio’s building will emerge. The ageing tract houses along the street are in varying states of repair, with trucks parked in front with mud on the bumpers from actual labor.

Avaio, which did not return a request for comment, projects that its 30-acre initial buildout would use 150MW of power – about the power consumption of 100,000 homes. The second phase would require up to a gigawatt of power, and consume about 4m gallons of water daily.

The neighbors are preparing as best they can for what’s coming. Activists have been passing out handbills calling on the neighborhood to attend the quorum court, the Arkansas equivalent of a county commission, to register objections. A recent hearing packed the chamber. But few people in the area – mostly Black or immigrants, mostly working class, often elderly – have the energy, or will, for sustained protest, the site’s neighbors say.

“Our government, who we choose to have represent us, can’t say no, regardless, even though we would want them to say no,” said Gale Jefferson, who lives near the proposed site. Her husband grew up in Wrightsville. They live on property that has been in their family for generations.

“A lot of this land is heir property. Their parents have died,” said Jefferson. “They don’t want to come back, but they don’t want to let go of the property. So there’s not a lot of people, per se.”

The community needs jobs, she said, gesturing toward the yellow sign on the boarded-up Dollar General at the end of the street, which wears a burial shroud of black latex. Jefferson fears the datacenter will probably employ no one from Wrightsville at all.

Avaio projected that its datacenter would produce 70 permanent jobs on the first phase of its buildout, said Wendell Griffen, a retired Arkansas circuit judge and court of appeals justice in Pulaski county, who won the Democratic primary in March to replace the county’s chief executive, Barry Hyde.

The site relies on a volunteer fire department that lacks specialized equipment, personnel, or commercially available fire-suppression foam needed to handle potential large-scale lithium-ion battery or electrical fires, Griffen said.

“This is very real redlining,” Griffen said. “It is appropriating rural, Black-owned land and converting it for industrial purposes, and it’s being done by people who have no historical or cultural tie to the land. These are not people who are local, developing their land for industrial use.

“These are people who are literally coming in, grabbing the land, industrializing it, but not to produce anything or give jobs in large measures to the people who are local inhabitants.”

Activists have been outraged by the revelation that the Pulaski county justice of the peace, Dianne Curry, had taken cues from an executive at energy firm Entergy Arkansas when drafting an exemption for Avaio from a proposed one-year development moratorium, which would have paused datacenter development in the county while leaders formulated better local regulations.

The Pulaski county quorum court last month rejected the proposed moratorium – and Avaio’s exemption – sending local lawmakers back to the table to find a way to constrain the development without running afoul of Arkansas state law against an outright ban.

Jefferson noted that her family’s property has no sewer line. Her neighbors are sensitive to electricity price changes, she said; most people run window cooling units in the summer because the houses don’t carry central air conditioning. She said she was concerned that her modest property could lose value.

But it’s what they’ve got. She’s trying to talk her husband into selling, she said.

In contrast to the county’s management of the datacenter issue, Little Rock’s municipal government passed an ordinance in June that set rigorous limits on how loud a hyperscale datacenter could be, how much heat it could generate, and how much water it could use, as well as sewerage and setbacks. It laid out financial penalties for non-compliance, and banned hyperscale datacenters from residential neighborhoods, essentially restricting any to the Little Rock Port Authority district.

Nonetheless, some residents called on the city to enact a broad moratorium on datacenters instead, to take more time to draft ordinances.

“To be fair, there are many people who are against the ordinance, saying they don’t feel like it’s as strong as they want it to be,” Scott said. “And then you talk to those who are for datacenters, they think it’s too strong…

“When you are a blue city leader in the midst of the red state, you have to figure out how to get in the middle, and still be progressive at the same time.”

Scott has a good personal relationship with the Arkansas governor, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Donald Trump’s former spokesperson, and daughter of former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee. Sanders and Scott got to know each other when they worked as political aides over the course of their careers – he for the former Democratic governor Mike Beebe, and she for Senator John Boozman.

“We’ve always had to interact with each other over the years, which is a good thing,” Scott said.

That helps mitigate the legislative threat from the state’s lawmakers, who view the city’s progressive politics with contempt. Little Rock’s lawyers wordsmithed their way through state law to provide as few footholds for a legal challenge to their datacenter ordinance – or future legislation – as they could.

“There’s a very hostile relationship between the state legislature and Little Rock, so much so that I do not – I mean, we hire a lobbyist to represent us – but I don’t step foot in there because I don’t want to bring too much attention,” said Scott. “There are states that are trying to take things away that cities own, because they’re literally considered a blue and a progressive city.”

title: Shifting left, Democrats see universal health care, taxing the rich as 'essential,' Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
description: Liberal Democrats now make up a clear majority of their party and view universal healthcare, greater abortion access and higher taxes on the rich as essential political
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Liberal Democrats now make up a clear majority of their party and view universal healthcare, greater abortion access and higher taxes on the rich as essential political positions, underscoring how Democrats have moved leftward in recent years, according to a ‌new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

The finding comes ahead of a Tuesday Democratic primary in which left-wing doctor Abdul El-Sayed is vying against moderate U.S. Representative ‌Haley Stevens for the party's nomination to run for a Michigan U.S. Senate seat. The seat is seen as critical for Democrats' hopes of winning a majority in that chamber in the ​November midterm elections.

The six-day poll, completed on Monday, showed the proportion of Democrats who label themselves as "liberal" has risen to 71% from 55% in 2012, while the share who see themselves as "conservative" has dwindled from 33% to 16%.

Some 76% of liberal Democrats said increasing taxes on corporations and billionaires was an "essential" policy position for anyone who considers themselves a liberal, the poll found. Another 72% said the same about expanding abortion access, while 71% said achieving government-provided healthcare for all Americans was a ‌necessary goal for any liberal.

Insurgent left-wing candidates ⁠this year have racked up a string of primary victories over more centrist Democrats, many of whom were backed by the party establishment. They have gone beyond New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's election last year in a deeply liberal city to ⁠vie for office in more politically divided states.

The Michigan primary is the latest example of that trend: Stevens is backed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and many top state Democrats, while El-Sayed was endorsed by liberal U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

Like Sanders, El-Sayed supports Medicare for All, a plan to provide public health insurance to ​all Americans ​that has become a rallying call for the insurgent left. Stevens supports strengthening subsidies ​for private health insurance.

In neighboring Wisconsin, another political swing state, ‌democratic socialist Francesca Hong appears poised to win the Democratic gubernatorial nomination despite efforts by party leaders to elevate a more moderate candidate.

The winner in Michigan will face the task of reuniting Democratic voters after a bitter primary campaign that was often dominated by the candidates' differences on Israel.

Stevens supports continued military funding for Israel and has benefited from tens of millions of dollars spent by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee backing her campaign. El-Sayed has been sharply critical of Israel, which he accuses of committing genocide in Gaza, and called for a halt to all aid.

Only 16% of Democrats support military and ‌economic support for Israel, while 57% oppose it, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll. Among liberal ​Democrats, more than 80% said reducing or eliminating that support was either important or essential ​for any liberal; only 18% said it was not important.

Some 89% of ​Republicans responding to the poll described themselves as conservative, a more modest shift from the 82% who labeled themselves that ‌way in the 2012 poll. Despite their near-unanimity around how to ​describe themselves, conservative Republicans were less unified ​in identifying policy goals as "essential."

Some 56% said allowing fewer immigrants into the country was an essential view for conservatives, a goal that has been central to President Donald Trump's rise to power and years in office. Similarly, only 50% of conservative Republicans said reducing the size of the ​federal government was essential to being conservative -- a goal ‌long pursued by conservative officeholders.

The poll, conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from 4,505 U.S. adults and had a margin of error ​of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 points for liberal Democrats and for conservative Republicans.

title: Manchin on supporting socialist candidate with ‘good ideas’: ‘Are you crazy?’
description: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Sunday shut down the idea of possibly supporting a socialist candidate in comments that come amid a recent rise of democratic socialists on the national political ...
fullText:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Sunday shut down the idea of possibly supporting a socialist candidate in comments that come amid a recent rise of democratic socialists on the national political stage.

During an appearance on CBS News's "Face the Nation," host Margaret Brennan asked about the possibility of backing a socialist candidate.

"No way, my God, no," Manchin said.

"Even if they have some good ideas?" Brennan pressed.

"I'll support the good ideas, but how could you support some of the crazy stuff they're for? Have you seen their platform?" Manchin responded.

"They're for dismantling everything that we know … whether it be the structure of government, Congress itself or the Senate, they want to get rid of. And then they start talking about all the crazy things: no police, no this, no this, no that," he added. "Are you crazy?"

Manchin's comments come as democratic socialist and left-leaning candidates notch wins in recent primaries, from the District of Columbia to California, New York and beyond. Within the last year, one of those primary winners, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), has become a superstar and one of the most talked-about members in his party.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), another prominent democratic socialist, has been discussed as a possible 2028 presidential contender.

title: Ferran on his MEGA cap: "Honestly, I know nothing about politics"
description: Barcelona striker, who may change clubs next season, told CNN his presence on Spain's victory parade at Cibeles in a cap echoing Trump's slogan was no big deal.View on euronews
fullText:
'Make America Great Again' (MAGA). The slogan, copied and reworked ad nauseam, even by groups hardly suspected of sharing Trumpist ideas, does not seem to have taken its toll on the Valencian Ferran Torres, who showed off a similar cap during the celebrations for La Roja's World Cup victories.

"It was just to have fun with my friends and family and it had nothing to do with politics," Torres said in English during an interview with 'CNN' after being asked about the initials on the cap, reworked as 'Make Spain Great Again'. "Honestly, I don't know anything about politics. It was only about being able to see Spain back on top again, winning the Cup."

The Trump administration, however, interpreted the forward's gesture as tacit support for the MAGA ideology, the populist wing of the Republicans rallying around the president. "Everyone wants to join this movement," the White House's official account even posted, a profile that since Trump's arrival has been used as a media loudspeaker for his circle.

Torres is reportedly in talks to leave Barça ahead of next season, amid rumours he could sign for Paris Saint-Germain, coached by Luis Enrique. CNN journalist Kaitlan Collins asked him directly about his future and PSG. "Right now the only thing I know is that I have to go back there on 12 August and train with them," the player said with a smile. "We'll see what happens (...) in football everything can change in an instant, I'm ready for anything."

The 26-year-old, born in 2000, scored the goal that secured the 2026 World Cup title against Argentina, in the 106th minute of the final played at the New York/New Jersey stadium. A day later, as reports were circulating that Torres owned a property company which had allegedly bought '20 homes in Valencia' to speculate with, he paraded the controversial cap during the victory parade held in Madrid. The player's entourage insisted that the story about the vulture fund was false.

'CNN' has not been the only studio Ferran Torres has appeared on during his stay in the United States, with further interviews scheduled on 'ESPN' and on NBC's Today show.

title: Analysis: Trump fumes as top allies back down on his personal battles
description: A president used to bending US politics to his will faces two stinging losses in a matter of days, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher.
fullText:
Watch: "She folded like an umbrella" - Trump attacks Jeanine Pirro over Reflecting Pool

It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.

In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.

From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making.

Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of contravening evidence.

Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.

"The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.

Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted – what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury – provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.

Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday.

"She folded like an umbrella," he groused.

If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.

'She folded like an umbrella' - Trump slams Jeanine Pirro over Reflecting Pool case

Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs

One of Trump's closest allies – his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche – was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.

Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.

Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.

Holdout senators back Blanche for AG after he formally withdraws Trump fund plan

In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund.

"It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.

The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.

In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.

Trump on Blanche: "He's going to do a great job"

While the Reflecting Pool prosecution and the so-called "anti-weaponisation fund" may be topics of intense presidential interest, they barely register as concerns for the larger American public.

That is decidedly not the case with the war with Iran, where Trump is once again accusing Iran of deceit amid another round of on-again, off-again negotiations and threats of overwhelming American military action.

On Monday, after asserting the previous day that he had called off "an attack that would have been the biggest attack since World War II" at the behest of Iranian officials and Arab intermediaries, Trump took to Truth Social to condemn what he said was Iranian duplicity after Iran denied any new direct negotiations.

"They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg', talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they're not having any discussions," Trump wrote.

If Iranians are misrepresenting the status of talks it wouldn't be the first time – but it also wouldn't be the first time Trump has seemingly taken their assurances at face value and heralded a new diplomatic breakthrough.

The latest twists in the war have become a familiar pattern with little progress, as polls continue to show American disapproval of the conflict and concern that Trump is not achieving his war goals.

Those recent public-opinion surveys suggest the war has become a growing drag on the president's overall popularity. A recent Associated Press poll puts Trump's approval at 33%, aligned with similar findings by CNN, Quinnipiac and YouGov. That matches or is below Trump's ratings after the Capitol riot and is above only Richard Nixon – who resigned from office in disgrace - among second-term US presidents in modern American history.

Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed surveys suggesting his historic unpopularity.

"My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been," he posted to Truth Social on Monday.

In three months, voters will head to the polls for congressional midterm elections. And Trump has shown surprising strength at the ballot box in the past, even in the face of seemingly daunting poll numbers.

While Trump may be grappling with – and, at times denying - recent adversity, that will be ultimate measure of his political fate. And if Republicans struggle, it may provide yet another reality that Trump, despite his best efforts, must eventially face.

title: Senate Republicans see Trump as a growing political liability
description: Senate Republicans say they see President Trump as a growing political liability as they try to hang on to control of the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, citing the president’s repeated attacks ...
fullText:
Senate Republicans say they see President Trump as a growing political liability as they try to hang on to control of the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, citing the president's repeated attacks on their ability to govern and his refusal to abandon a proposed $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund for MAGA allies.

GOP senators also warn that Trump's relentless demands that the Senate pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act before the election, even though it has little to no chance of becoming law, risk "demoralizing" the Republican base.

And they fear Trump's refusal to abandon the $1.8 billion compensation fund for MAGA allies is playing into Democratic political attacks that the Trump administration is corrupt.

New polls showing Republican candidates trailing their Democratic challengers in North Carolina and GOP-leaning states including Ohio, Iowa and Texas underscore what GOP senators and the leadership see as a need to push back against Trump on key issues.

One Republican senator, who requested anonymity to discuss colleagues' views of Trump's sinking approval rating and his impact on congressional races, said fellow GOP senators view Trump as a growing political liability.

"That's the perception in the room," the lawmaker said of the discussion within the Senate GOP conference, noting that even Republican colleagues in rock-solid red states such as Sen. Roger Marshall (Kan.) may have to sweat out close races.

Some Republican senators think Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) — who's running for reelection in Nebraska, another farm state hit hard by the Trump economy — could be vulnerable against independent challenger Dan Osborn.

Trump won Kansas and Nebraska by 16 points and 20 points, respectively, but since then his job approval rating has steadily dropped, especially among self-identified independents, who are shifting away from the Republican Party in significant numbers.

Several other Republican incumbents face tough reelections, including Sens. Susan Collins in Maine, Jon Husted in Ohio and Dan Sullivan in Alaska, and colleagues say they're battling major headwinds caused by Trump's low approval ratings.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Trump's refusal to abandon the $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund, which was set up to pay MAGA allies who were prosecuted or investigated during the Biden administration, has become a political "yoke" hampering GOP colleagues and candidates ahead of the November election.

Tillis called Trump's resistance to permanently quashing the fund "horrible policy" and "horrible politics."

"I want this yoke off of the members who are up for election in November because there's no way to explain it, no way to explain it whatsoever," he said.

"This is going to lend credibility to the Democrats hanging this on the necks of Republicans who are up in November," he warned. "Why we're not taking this off the table — it's not helping the president's popularity; it's not helping our candidates who are up for reelection. Nothing good is coming from this."

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Justice Department issued a statement late Sunday rescinding the order that established the $1.8 billion fund after Tillis and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) threatened to block Blanche's nomination to serve in a longer-term capacity as attorney general.

The Justice Department in its statement noted that Blanche had "repeatedly advised Congress through testimony and in written responses that the fund would not be moving forward," but Cornyn and Tillis told reporters that someone at the White House had resisted revising Trump's settlement with the Justice Department to permanently eliminate the fund.

Despite the late-night settlement to end the debate over the "anti-weaponization" fund, Republicans have worried for months that the proposal could give Democrats powerful political ammo in campaigns.

Tillis earlier suggested that Republican Michael Whatley, who is running for Tillis's North Carolina Senate seat, would be wise to find ways to distance himself from Trump.

"He's going to have to have almost a perfect — 10, spot-the-landing — campaign to overcome the headwinds," he said.

Asked if Whatley should distance himself from Trump, Tillis said, "I don't want him to be artificial, but if there are things that he thinks that he would do differently, I think he should have the courage to speak up."

"If he believes, for example, the 1776 fund was a bad idea, he should speak up about it. I know in North Carolina most people think it's a bad idea," he said, referring to the $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund.

Tillis is retiring at the end of the term.

A White House spokesperson pushed back on the criticism from GOP senators and touted Trump's accomplishments since taking office.

"President Trump is the unequivocal leader of the Republican party who is committed to maintaining Republicans' majority in Congress. In just over one year, the President has made our country greater than ever before with the most secure border in American history, the largest middle-class tax cuts ever, and the lowest murder rate since 1900," said White House spokesperson Olivia Wales.

The White House aide said Trump has drawn a "sharp contrast" with Democrats on immigration and keeping communities safe.

"President Trump will continue to draw a sharp contrast with his commonsense agenda and the radical Democrats in Congress who allowed millions of illegal aliens to flow through the border, unanimously opposed the Working Families Tax Cuts, and are soft-on-crime," Wales said.

Republican senators have also criticized Trump's push to secure taxpayer funding for a new 90,000-square-foot ballroom at the White House. GOP lawmakers stripped $1 billion in funding for the ballroom from a $70 billion budget reconciliation package that the Senate passed in June.

GOP senators say Trump's increasingly sharp criticism of the Senate's failure to pass the SAVE America Act is likely to demoralize the Republican base.

And they warn that Trump's comments hinting at dissatisfaction with Senate Majority Leader John Thune's (R-S.D.) job performance are undercutting the message to voters that the Senate Republican majority tallied up big accomplishments for the American people.

Republican lawmakers were especially frustrated over Trump's lack of enthusiasm for the housing affordability bill they passed and touted as an important response to rising home costs.

Trump has seemed ambivalent about whether Thune should keep his job as leader. Asked if Thune is the man for the job, Trump answered, "Well, we're going to find out, and I'll let you know."

At a recent rally in Georgia, Trump fumed the Senate "is a place you send things when you want them to die" and warned "we're not going to take this any longer."

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said that kind of talk from the president when Republicans are in control of Congress "doesn't help."

"I've been out there a good bit in the various battleground states, and I think … most Americans think that Washington, including but not limited to Congress, is dysfunctional anyway," he said. "But I don't think it helps. It doesn't help. And I wish there was some way to lessen the president's frustration."

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said Trump's increasingly harsh criticism of the GOP-controlled Senate "doesn't help."

"It's so unfortunate because it doesn't help John," she said, referring to Thune. "He has a hard enough job herding the cats that he has. When you have a president that is publicly challenging his leadership, that makes his job harder."

"And then the president says, 'Go out and unify all of your Republicans.' Well, sir, you have just caused greater disruption among the conference. It doesn't help us," she said.

Murkowski marveled at the escalating tensions between the White House and GOP senators in recent weeks.

"It certainly doesn't give the appearance that there is good communication coming from the president and the administration with Congress, and that's a problem. Supposedly we're all supposed to be on the same page," she said.

Cornyn warned that Trump and his allies on Capitol Hill, who are insisting that the Senate cancel the August recess to debate the SAVE America Act, are likely to leave conservative voters disappointed and thus less likely to turn out to vote in November.

The Texas senator singled out Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) for criticism.

"He's demoralizing our base of voters we're depending on in 99 days to elect Republicans," he said.

Cornyn last week also expressed bewilderment over Trump escalating the battle over the "anti-weaponization" fund, something that could have derailed Blanche's nomination to serve as attorney general.

"I frankly don't understand why they're trying to escalate the fight," he said Thursday.

Cornyn confirmed in a statement from his spokesperson on Sunday night that he had reached a deal to permanently eliminate the fund and set the parameters of Trump's settlement with the Justice Department and IRS more clearly.

"Sen. Cornyn has reached an agreement with the Department of Justice, which will be issuing a formal order permanently terminating the anti-weaponization fund and making clear in a binding written document that the scope of the audit settlement is limited to only the plaintiffs, including the President, and the IRS," said Cornyn spokesperson Natalie Yezbick.

Trump on Saturday said he planned to keep Blanche in the role of acting attorney general as he presses for Congress to authorize the $1.8 billion fund.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who lost his primary election earlier this year after Trump endorsed his opponent, defended Thune from Trump's criticism.

He said Trump could play a more constructive role by helping Thune whip votes within the Senate GOP conference instead of "blaming" Senate Republicans for not getting their jobs done.

"Everybody has to be in it together; you can't just point fingers," he said.

"We got things that we need to pass, like a farm bill. It would be really great if we focused on passing the farm bill. Good policy is good politics," he said. "That's the important thing we should all be focused on, including the president."

Another of the top risers on the FTSE 100 this morning is Sainsbury’s. The supermarket chain is up 4% after it said it had agreed the £120m sale of catalogue shopping business Argos to a trio of retail veterans – a decade after buying the company for more than £1bn.

Sainsbury’s said it would be able to fully focus on its core food business and “creating a simpler business with higher margins, higher growth and stronger free cash flow generation”.

The supermarket bought Argos as part of Home Retail Group in 2016, but its hopes to take on Amazon and John Lewis have foundered. Sainsbury’s boss Simon Roberts decided to about turn when he took over in 2020, focusing on food, which has much higher barriers to entry for Amazon or other Chinese players because of the cold chain logistics required to keep food fresh.

Sainsbury’s had considered a Chinese buyer for Argos a year ago.

The supermarket said it had reached long-term commercial agreements with Argos, including rental income for Argos stores inside Sainsbury’s and income relating to the Nectar360 and Nectar loyalty schemes.

The buyer will be Swift Partners, new company established for the deal by former Co-operative supermarket chief executive Richard Pennycook, former Morrisons executive Trevor Strain and banker Matt Truman.

What attracted us to Argos is the strength of the business, with a trusted brand, loyal customers and dedicated colleagues. We believe strongly in Argos’s future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress.

Argos’s combination - of a strong digital business supported by standalone stores, stores inside Sainsbury’s and local fulfilment centres - gives it a distinctive position in the market and an excellent platform for growth.

title: Analysis-Japan PM's political doom loop worsens her fight with markets
description: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is fighting a losing battle in the polls, making a retreat from promised tax cuts more difficult
fullText:
TOKYO, July 29 (Reuters) - Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is fighting a losing battle in the polls, making a retreat from promised tax cuts more difficult and denying her officials the political backup they need to talk down yen and bond market bears.

Takaichi's approval rating slumped in July to the lowest since she took office last year ‌as rising inflation, blamed in part on high import costs from a weak yen, hit her standing with voters.

The prime minister's strong advocacy of fiscal stimulus and harsh criticism of higher interest rates ‌have heightened investor concerns about worsening public finances in Japan, sending bond yields higher.

Those bond market anxieties have also blunted official efforts to talk down speculative bets against the yen, government sources said.

"Markets are gaining control over fiscal management, which hasn't happened in Japan for ​decades," one of them said, warning about the danger of being at the mercy of bond vigilantes.

Since becoming prime minister last year, Takaichi has sought to pursue a pro-growth agenda while also tempering investor concerns about fiscal discipline and central bank independence.

Those competing demands have created a communication challenge that has at times led to unwanted market volatility, which in turn makes policy implementation more difficult.

For example, her spending plans, aimed in part at easing rising household living costs, lifted bond yields to three-decade highs in July on concern over Japan's worsening finances.

Mindful of such market pressures, Takaichi told a news briefing on Monday the administration would seek to gain market trust in Japan's finances through ‌transparent communication.

"I would say communication with markets would become more important," she said ⁠when asked what she could have done better.

But when pressed about her administration's sliding approval ratings, Takaichi stressed her determination to break Japan's "excessive fiscal tightening" with big investment, a sign she had no plans to back down on expansionist policy.

"The sliding approval ratings would only solidify the premier's determination to cut tax and boost investment," another source ⁠said. "Pursuing her policies would jolt markets, while not doing so would hit her popularity. It's a dilemma."

Those challenges could worsen ahead of a host of events that could ignite a renewed spike in yields.

Despite reservations voiced even within her ruling party, Takaichi is set to proceed with a plan to cut by two years an 8% levy on food, domestic media reported. While the move would come as little surprise, a lack of funding clarity could further upset bond markets, analysts say.

title: Joe Rogan warns liberals against trying to turn Texas blue, says it would wreck the state's 'delicate balance'

fullText:
Podcaster Joe Rogan warned liberals Tuesday that moving to Texas and turning the state blue would ruin the delicate balance for everybody, including liberal Texans.

"The liberals that want to turn Texas blue, like, don't. You're going to ruin it," he said.

Rogan, a former Californian, has spoken out numerous times about his choice to leave California over its far-left policies, particularly those from the COVID-19 pandemic years.

Coastal Workers Fleeing Blue Strongholds Could Create An Opportunity For Detroit

Rogan lamented that many "coastal elites" and "coastal snobs" often "have this idea of it being filled with rednecks and ignorant people and foolish people. It's not that way at all. Especially Austin. Austin is like one of the most, like, liberal, easygoing, progressive cities, but even the progressives here, they're like, more reasonable."

He specified that liberal Texans, while they shifted somewhat leftward in recent years, are nowhere near the same far-left positions as those of Los Angeles or New York.

"There's this saying about Austin: 'Keep Austin Weird … and surrounded,'" Rogan said.

"And surrounded? What is the 'and surrounded?'" guest Forrest Galante asked.

"Surrounded by red people. Like it's all red states around you, and it's this pocket of blue that's in the center of this red state," Rogan said. "I think that's good for everybody. I think that's good. It's a balance."

Rogan warned against liberals fleeing blue states only to vote for the same left-wing policies. He compared the state's delicate political balance to that of an ecosystem.

"You're going to ruin it," he warned. "You're going to ruin it for you too. You don't get it. Balance is important. … You can't kill all the predators because then the deer get overrun, and you're hitting them with cars. And you can't kill all the deer because then there's no food. That's what they did when they were market hunting. Balance. And you need balance with humans, too.

"The Austin balance is a great balance," Rogan continued. "It's a liberal city surrounded by, like, hardcore Republicans with guns and tigers."

Joe Rogan Mocks Gavin Newsom For Dismissing Growing State Problems As La Film Production Craters

In 2023, Rogan noted that he got the idea to leave amid the riots in 2020 after the death of Minneapolis resident George Floyd.

"I was like, 'This ain't going in a good direction, and I f---ing smell chaos," he said.

More recently, in 2026, he blasted California Gov. Gavin Newsom for his defense of California, warning instead that Los Angeles may go the way of Detroit as the film industry implodes and companies flee the state.

The latest IRS migration data show Texas is seeing billions of dollars in taxpayer wealth flowing into the state, while Census figures show the state's largest metropolitan areas continue to outpace much of the country in population growth.

Dallas-Fort Worth added more residents than any metropolitan area in the country over the past year, while Houston, Austin and San Antonio also ranked among the nation's fastest-growing metros.

fullText:
New York Times reporter Jonathan Swan suggested during a "60 Minutes Australia" interview released last week that President Donald Trump has "Napoleonic" ambition and a political survivability that should humble journalists.

Swan and fellow Times reporter Maggie Haberman discussed their new book, "Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump," and Swan offered speculation on the rest of the president's term and cautioned other journalists to have some humility.

"So there's still a sense that, even if Democrats take the House from Trump, they really can't touch him," Swan said in the interview. "And, like you said, his family's made a lot of money. He's wealthier than he's ever been. He has immunity conferred by the Supreme Court. And there's no prospect, even if he does get impeached, there's no prospect of a conviction."

"I think Donald Trump's obituary has been written so many times — his political obituary — by so many people," Swan continued. "And by this point, if you don't have some humility around that, I think, you know, you're operating in a fairly delusional way. This is someone who has incredible survival capacities, who's able to regenerate himself, and he's still got two and a half years left as the most powerful man on the planet, with no intention of receding at all."

How Trump Survives: Battling The Media, Former Allies And Assassination Attempts

As he spoke about the future of Trump's term, he noted that the president's next step may be taking on the Cuban regime.

"So there are many things he could do," he said. "The most obvious in foreign policy is Cuba. They've been looking at potential regime change in Cuba, but who knows? It's a big world out there, and we don't want to start being pundits and prognosticating."

Swan also described a past encounter at the White House that he suggested speaks volumes about Trump's personal mindset and policies. As Trump met with Swan and Haberman, he had purportedly shown them a document he claimed was written by a historian.

"So it opens by saying Donald Trump is the most powerful man who's ever existed, ever lived on the planet, by far," Swan said. "And then it goes on to compare him to what Donald Trump said was, to us, the top ten. And it was Stalin, Mao, Hitler, Napoleon, Attila the Hun, Genghis Khan, the Caesars, Alexander the Great, Tamerlane ... there's probably one I'm missing."

Trump Aims To Reset War Powers Clock With Controversial Bid To Bypass Congress

"And it had nothing to do with morality," Swan continued. "The document didn't mention morality. It was about power and raw power."

The premise of the document, Swan said, was that Trump is the most powerful leader in history and is willing to use power in a way no previous president has done within their lifetime, which he noted was remarkably similar to the book he wrote about the administration.

Swan added further, "I think it's also that he wants to be a sort of Napoleonic ... you know, the person who only needs to be known by one name, who is the defining figure of our age. And so, when Trump thinks about himself in history, I don't think he's comparing himself to Bill Clinton or, you know, name your U.S. president — Eisenhower. I think it is to figures like Napoleon and that he wants to be the defining global figure of our age."

The only legacy President Trump is concerned with is making America greater than ever before."

title: Fact check: Trump is approaching 10 years of telling his Michigan ‘Man of the Year’ lie
description: For three consecutive presidential campaigns, President Donald Trump regularly told the same lie when he spoke in the swing state of Michigan. Before he even entered politics, he claimed, he was named...
fullText:
For three consecutive presidential campaigns, President Donald Trump regularly told the same lie when he spoke in the swing state of Michigan. Before he even entered politics, he claimed, he was named "Man of the Year" in the state.

The problem: CNN and other media outlets repeatedly noted that this award did not exist. But Trump revived the tale once more near the end of a falsehood-filled economic speech in Michigan on Monday — and added an additional lie claiming that an initially skeptical media had eventually discovered the award story was correct.

"I was here 25 years ago, I got Man of the Year. They — oh, by the way, the press questioned that, and then they found out it was true, actually," Trump said with a chuckle. "And I made a speech, and all I talked about was why are you letting them steal your auto industry?"

Nope. This is yet another example of the fake history that has littered various Trump addresses this month.

Approaching 10 full years after Trump debuted the "Man of the Year" lie, nobody has ever been able to find any evidence for it. The state of Michigan does not give out a "Man of the Year" award, Trump has never lived in the state, and he and his team have never specified who or what entity supposedly gave him this award and when.

In 2023, after nearly seven years of debunkings of Trump's "Man of the Year" tales, a Republican group in Michigan created a "Man of the Decade" award and gave it to him.

But Trump made clear Monday that this is not what he was referring to, since he said he was talking about a "Man of the Year" honor he received decades ago. (Side note: in many previous tellings of the "Man of the Year" story, like one during his 2024 campaign, he has placed the supposed honor in the 2010s rather than the 2000s as he suggested Monday.)

Dave Trott, a former Republican congressman in Michigan who became a sharp critic of Trump, has offered the most plausible theory about the possible basis for Trump's made-up story. In 2019, Trott contacted CNN to note that Trump had suggested at an event two years prior that he had received the "Man of the Year" award at a 2013 Republican dinner in Michigan to which Trott had invited Trump to make a speech.

At that 2013 dinner, Trott gave Trump gifts that included a framed copy of the Gettysburg Address. But Trott emphatically noted that nobody gave Trump any "Man of the Year" award.

At least once, Trump has acknowledged that the idea of him receiving such an honor in Michigan before his time as a politician was bewildering.

"In fact, five or six years before I even thought about running, for whatever reason they named me Man of the Year in Michigan. I said, 'How come?' I didn't even understand it myself," he said at a 2019 rally in New Hampshire — then repeated, "But I was named Man of the Year."

title: The UK’s first TikTok PM? Andy Burnham channels Zohran Mamdani as he hits social media

Before Burnham stepped inside No 10 this week he promised to “do things differently” in British politics. If his feed is anything to go by, he’s already way ahead of his predecessor.

fullText:
From Mo Farah to Bus Aunty, new prime minister makes good on promise to ‘do things differently’ when it comes to communication

They say a week is a long time in politics, but handily for followers of Andy Burnham on social media, you can get daily updates of what the new PM has been up to on his timeline.

Before Burnham stepped inside No 10 this week he promised to “do things differently” in British politics. If his feed is anything to go by, he’s already way ahead of his predecessor.

Burnham’s social media team have done away with the buttoned-up operation of Keir Starmer, opting instead for a style that has already drawn comparisons to another much more “online” politician: the mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani.

Burnham’s TikTok page this week has revealed him to be a man (or at least a man who pays someone) who enjoys a meme, someone who comments with emojis, collaborates with influencers and chats policy while pouring a pint.

Noticeable were the policy announcements shot in primarily vertical videos, ideal for mobile phone consumption on TikTok, Facebook and Instagram.

“He’s gone all in on the TikTok style,” said Andrew Chadwick, professor of political communication at Loughborough University. “So far, he’s had some very simple, clear policy pledges that cut through.”

During the lead-up to his first day in No 10, Burnham’s team also released a 2.5-minute video of Burnham inviting people in Cardiff to “ask Andy anything” from addressing homelessness and social care to supporting pubs and the hospitality sector.

Searches for “Andy Burnham” on TikTok surged by more than 2,000% day on day in the UK when he became prime minister on Monday.

Burnham started off his first day with a handheld video outside a centre for the London-based homelessness charity The Passage, promising to end rough sleeping “at the first opportunity”. A “day one” montage posted later on, showing him inside The Passage, meeting his cabinet and speaking outside No 10, received more than 820,000 views.

His team also posted two prepackaged videos starring influencers and celebrities. Burnham joined Sir Mo Farah for a jog through London as part of the gold medallist’s YouTube series Run With Mo, which was reposted on Farah’s Instagram to his 1.9 million followers.

Social media is about content, of course but it’s also a numbers game. Burnham’s team showed that when they had him take part in the viral Career Ladder series, hosted by Ukrainian internet personality Max Klymenko, who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

These collaboration deals offer Burnham “exposure” to new audiences and build a “constructed sense of authenticity” on the platform, said Chadwick. “Burnham has a brand to construct here. OK, big in the north-west of England, absolutely. But among most people, who don’t follow politics particularly closely, he’s got hard work to do.”

The world of social media is all about taking ideas and riffing on them – and imitation is, after all, the sincerest form of flattery, but one video from Burnham’s first week of posts showed just the kind of online profile he’d like to emulate.

The PM’s video on Wednesday, announcing his plans to cut VAT on energy bills – one of the more eye-catching in his week one policy blitz – received more than 1m views. Keen-eyed political watchers, however, spotted a similarity between his announcement video and one posted by Zohran Mamdani some months back.

The video, which starts with Burnham tapping the camera and stepping backward, references a video by Mamdani who in April used the same move to announce his pied-à-terre tax.

Those behind Mamdani’s digital strategy have taken note. “I think it’s great that he’s not shying away from these direct, creative references, while also doing some creative things of his own,” said Debbie Saslaw, co-founder of the political ad agency Melted Solids with Anthony DiMieri.

But Saslaw also has a warning for Burnham: “I saw, during the campaign, he jumped on a lot of Instagram meme trends. Stay away from that. That’s something that becomes automatically cringe, no matter who does it.”

In his first week as PM, Burnham’s TikTok following rose by approximately 73%, from just under 99,000 to more than 170,000, according to consultancy Knox Digital. In terms of engagement, Burnham narrowly beat Starmer’s first week on TikTok in December 2025, at 6.29% to the previous PM’s 6.23%.

“There is an authentic style that comes through” in Burnham’s videos, said Andrew Bard Epstein, the communications director on Mamdani’s election campaign. “Where it feels different, substantively, from Zohran is the ambition of the agenda.”

He added: “In terms of style and authenticity, he is clearing the very low bar left by Keir Starmer. But unless it is matched with some stronger stuff – on confronting concentrated power, inequality and a diminishing quality of life in a way that feels like it meets the scale of the crisis – I wonder if people may grow tired of it.”

title: A Turkish governor is sacked over photos in snug cycling shorts. Many want him reinstated
description: A cycling-enthusiast governor rode into an unexpected political storm in Turkey when he found himself sacked after photos of him in snug cycling shorts went viral.  Mehmet Fatih Cicekli, the governor ...
fullText:
ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — A cycling-enthusiast governor rode into an unexpected political storm in Turkey when he found himself sacked after photos of him in snug cycling shorts went viral. He has since also become the center of a campaign pressing for his return to office amid an outpouring of affection.

Mehmet Fatih Cicekli, the governor of Ardahan province in eastern Turkey, was removed from his post on July 17 by a presidential decree signed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. While no reason was given for his dismissal, it came after some Turkish politicians criticized him for wearing cycling tights during a public event promoting the sport and for posting the photos on social media.

Inan Akgun Alp, a member of the main opposition Republican People's Party, accused Cicekli of allegedly prioritizing social media over official duties, adding the tight attire was inappropriate for a governor.

"He goes around in tights, spends all day cycling, with bodyguards in front of him, cycling in tights until the evening," the T-24 news website quoted Alp as saying during a parliamentary debate last week. "A governor cannot wander around the city center like this."

Samil Tayyar, a former legislator from Erdogan's ruling party, which has roots in Turkey's Islamic movement, said the attire was contrary to cultural norms, especially in a conservative, traditional province like Ardahan. He argued that other politicians wore sweatpants while cycling.

"People can wear whatever they want in their private lives, but a governor cannot visit the public in tights while on duty; it does not align with the seriousness of the state. In a traditional social setting like Ardahan, it is completely unacceptable," Tayyar wrote on X.

Cicekli, who was appointed governor in January by Erdogan, defended himself by arguing that what he wore was normal cycling attire.

"(We will) keep pedaling. I am an athlete who practices sailing, rowing and cycling. The clothes I'm wearing are sportswear," T-24 quoted him as saying.

A petition campaign to try and get him reinstated has gathered more than 10,000 signatures, with supporters arguing that the governor was engaged in important work in Ardahan, promoting sports, youth activities and bicycle tourism, the opposition-leaning Halk TV reported.

In an emotional farewell to his supporters in Ardahan on Wednesday, Cicekli said: "I believe that I have not let down those who vouched for me and stood by me throughout my journey until now. I believe that this is the greatest honor of all."

As he left Ardahan, a province that borders both Armenia and Georgia, local cyclists accompanied his vehicle to send him off as a show of support, Halk TV reported.

Nacho Sánchez Amor, a member of the European Parliament from Spain who serves as the rapporteur on Turkey, expressed support for Cicekli and suggested Alp was promoting the ruling party's "Islamist conservative agenda."

title: Elon Musk says he got ‘carried away’ with Trump – but still holds on to contentious political views
description:
In interview, billionaire says instead of running ‘Doge’ he should’ve ‘worked on my companies’ and shares extreme predictions
Elon Musk has admitted he became too consumed by politics during his volatile alliance with Donald Trump and his brief appointment as the president’s financial axman, running the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge).
The world’s richest person, and briefly its first trillionaire after his SpaceX company floated on the New York stock exchange in June, made the confession in a wide-ranging interview with the Economist published on Thursday. He shared his positions on subjects from foreign wars to AI, and made a number of eye-opening predictions for the future.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
In interview, billionaire says instead of running ‘Doge’ he should’ve ‘worked on my companies’ and shares extreme predictions

Elon Musk has admitted he became too consumed by politics during his volatile alliance with Donald Trump and his brief appointment as the president’s financial axman, running the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge).

The world’s richest person, and briefly its first trillionaire after his SpaceX company floated on the New York stock exchange in June, made the confession in a wide-ranging interview with the Economist published on Thursday. He shared his positions on subjects from foreign wars to AI, and made a number of eye-opening predictions for the future.

“I got carried away, frankly,” Musk said of his relationship with the president, whom he helped get elected in 2024 with $200m in financial backing, then served during his controversial tenure as head of Doge, overseeing $150bn in “harmful” budget cuts and forcing tens of thousands of people out of federal jobs.

The owner of Tesla did not expand on the statement, but appeared cognizant of the impact of his dalliance with the levers of power in Washington DC.

In December, he offered in a podcast with Katie Miller, wife of Trump’s White House adviser Stephen Miller, that his wrecking-ball approach to the federal government had been only partially successful, and that given the opportunity he probably wouldn’t do it again.

“I think instead of doing Doge, I would have basically worked on my companies,” he said at the time.

Talking to the Economist, however, he appeared to relish the attention his political involvement had garnered, and the influence he believed he exerted. “People don’t realize that what I’m saying will come to pass,” he said, the outlet referring to Musk – at least in his own mind – as a modern-day Cassandra.

The interview, a 90-minute conversation for the publication’s video platform The Insider, recorded at a Tesla factory in Texas, was Musk’s first since the SpaceX flotation, in which his personal wealth briefly topped $1.25tn before dropping back to a relatively penurious $750bn.

He reflected on moving from “exhilaration to terror” in a single day, but was not referring to the SpaceX share price. Instead, he was talking about artificial intelligence, which he believes will ultimately render work by humans “optional”.

AI systems and robots will eventually handle most digital and physical jobs, he said, and the merger of his own AI venture with SpaceX will allow him to develop systems to perform cognitive tasks such as software programming while Tesla manufactures humanoids.

Musk, the Economist said, plans to power his AI venture with datacenters in space, which experts have warned will be “catastrophic” for Earth.

Within five years, Musk said, AI intelligence systems may surpass the sum of all human intelligence. Within 10 years, robots in the workplace will help usher in an era of such “amazing abundance” that money will become meaningless.

It was, however, Musk’s political views, and predictions, that were perhaps the most contentious parts of the interview. The UK, a country he has not visited for years, but whose politics, especially on immigration and race, have become a recent obsession, will become engulfed in a civil war within 20 years, he claimed.

Asked if he was anti-Muslim, Musk attacked the questioner, a policy of diversion similar to that which has served Trump well, and which he has employed previously, notably calling the Guardian “irrelevant” when it decided to withdraw from his “toxic” social media platform X.

“I’m against rape and murder. I’m against the imposition of rules and laws that are contrary to what we’ve come to accept in the west,” he said. “It’s a crying shame that traditional media, like you, don’t recognize this.”

He described the media’s characterization of Europe’s far right as “false, misleading and nonsense”, and argued that it was made up of “normal people” seeking safe cities, secure borders and sensible spending, the Economist said.

In an analysis piece accompanying the interview, the outlet acknowledged that Musk was a divisive figure. “His political views, disseminated to his 240m followers on X, strike many as plain-speaking and strike many more, including The Economist, as plainly bigoted,” it wrote.

“But he is also one of a handful of men who are pioneering AI and who thereby have an outsize influence on its trajectory. When he speaks, he reflects the debates they are having. His datacentres in space could power AI’s future.

“For all his political polemics, he has a record of being right about technology in fields such as electric cars, rockets and satellite communications that confounded other engineers and entrepreneurs.”

Another Musk prediction: after AI destroys jobs, there may need to be a large-scale wealth redistribution to create “universal high income” for humans.

He said he would be willing to pay “trillions in tax” then, conversely, argued that money will become irrelevant inside 10 years. In which eventuality, he said, governments should “issue people cheques”, because, he said, amid an infinite supply of goods and services produced by machines, deflation will be a bigger problem than inflation.

He also shared thoughts about the Ukraine war, in which his Starlink satellites have been used to help that country’s military against Russia’s aggression. Despite this, Musk said any peace deal should include territorial gains for Russia.

The interview concluded with an assessment by Musk of his achievements and ambitious current projects, in AI and in space, a field in which he has also made a number of bold predictions. He said in 2024 that humans could set foot on Mars by 2028 (currently Nasa is targeting 2028 for a return to the moon, which many analysts think is unlikely).

The universe, Musk said, according to the Economist, could be a computer simulation created by aliens. “The things I’m doing are so preposterous that it’s hard to believe they’re real,” he said.

title: Lindell, Tafoya widening leads in Minnesota GOP primaries: Poll
description: A new poll shows both businessman Mike Lindell and political and cultural commentator Michele Tafoya gaining momentum in the Minnesota Republican gubernatorial and Senate primaries, respectively. The ...
fullText:
A new poll shows both businessman Mike Lindell and political and cultural commentator Michele Tafoya gaining momentum in the Minnesota Republican gubernatorial and Senate primaries, respectively.

The poll, conducted by KSTP/SurveyUSA, shows that while the GOP frontrunners are gaining bigger leads, the Democratic Senate primary between Rep. Angie Craig (Minn.) and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is still tightening.

Lindell leads the Republican gubernatorial primary by 9 points, with 35 percent of support, according to the poll. House Speaker Lisa Demuth is in second place with 26 percent, and GOP-endorsed Kendall Qualls is in third with 11 percent. Twenty-two percent of respondents were undecided. Lindell recently received a "complete and total" endorsement from President Trump, calling him "one of America's greatest and most hard working patriots" in a post on Truth Social.

A federal judge in Minnesota ruled against the "Pillow Man" last year over his claims that Smartmatic voting machines helped rig the 2020 presidential election.

In the last month, Lindell selected Phillip Parish, a retired Navy lieutenant commander, for his running mate after Parish ended his own Republican gubernatorial campaign.

Candidates want to flip the Minnesota governor seat from Tim Walz (D), who after two terms will not be seeking reelection. The former vice president hopeful came under heavy criticism for his handling of the state's fraud scandal.

Prosecutors alleged as much as $9 billion was stolen by various groups in reimbursements for meal assistance aid and other services.

The Minnesota Republican Senate Primary has Tafoya leading by around 30 points, with 41 percent of the vote. She hopes to flip retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith's seat.

Royce White, the former professional basketball player who previously ran for state Senate came in second place with 10 percent of support; Tom Weiler, a Navy veteran who previously ran for the House received 7 percent; Adam Schwarze, a combat veteran backed by the Minnesota GOP, received 5 percent. Twenty-eight percent of respondents were undecided.

The Minnesota primaries will be held on Aug. 11.

title: Almost half say Supreme Court rulings on Trump agenda based on politics: Survey
description: Nearly half of Americans say they believe the Supreme Court is ruling on President Trump’s policies based on ideology instead of the law, according to a new poll. The Washington Post/Ipsos survey, con...
fullText:
Nearly half of Americans say they believe the Supreme Court is ruling on President Trump's policies based on ideology instead of the law, according to a new poll.

The Washington Post/Ipsos survey, conducted July 8-13, found that 46 percent of 2,648 respondents said they believe the nine justices are ruling on cases impacting the president's agenda based on ideology.

A quarter of respondents said the high court is ruling on those cases based on the law, while 28 percent had no opinion and 1 percent skipped the question.

The Supreme Court has given Trump multiple unfavorable rulings during his second term. The high court in February struck down emergency tariffs the president issued on imports last year and invalidated his Day 1 executive order restricting birthright citizenship last month.

But the high court has also ruled in the president's favor, including when it allowed him to fire Democrat Rebecca Slaughter from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). The 6-3 decision, handed down along ideological lines, overturned the high court's 1935 decision in Humphrey's Executor v. United States — which afforded certain executive branch agencies a degree of independence from the White House for 91 years.

Under the latest ruling, the president has increased authority over federal agencies, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor writing the decision grants "far greater power than ever before" to Trump and future occupants of the Oval Office.

"It is true that today's decision does not  eliminate the FTC or the many other agencies whose structures are implicated by overruling Humphrey's," Sotomayor wrote in her dissent, joined by fellow liberal Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson. "It is undeniable, however, that those agencies will be transformed in ways that those who created them never could have expected and actively sought to avoid, fundamentally recalibrating the balance of power in this country in the process."

After the high court's term ended in late June, Trump said the Slaughter ruling was the "biggest and most consequential decision" it issued.

Overall, 55 percent of respondents to the Washington Post/Ipsos survey disapproved of the way the Supreme Court is doing its job. Just more than 4 in 10 respondents approved of the high court, while 4 percent skipped the question.

Respondents' views toward the Supreme Court were divided along partisan lines, with 75 percent of Democrats disapproving and 67 percent of Republicans approving. Just less than 6 in 10 respondents, meanwhile, disapproved of the court.

The survey had a margin of error of 1.9 percentage points.

title: Mercedes engine claim piles pressure on FIA while Red Bull pushes for sweeping wing ban
description: Formula 1's political battle over the 2026 regulations has intensified on two fronts, with Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff making a striking admission about his team's power unit while Red Bull reportedly pushes the FIA to introduce a blanket ban on rotating rear-wing concepts. The developments come at a crucial stage of the season, with the FIA's second Assessment of Dynamic Unit Output (ADUO) measurement period set to close after the Hungarian Grand Prix.
fullText:
Formula 1's political battle over the 2026 regulations has intensified on two fronts, with Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff making a striking admission about his team's power unit while Red Bull reportedly pushes the FIA to introduce a blanket ban on rotating rear-wing concepts.

The developments come at a crucial stage of the season, with the FIA's second Assessment of Dynamic Unit Output (ADUO) measurement period set to close after the Hungarian Grand Prix. The deadline could prove pivotal in determining whether any intervention is required to balance performance before the sport enters its new engine era in 2026.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Wolff appeared to contradict the FIA's current assessment by declaring that Mercedes has "the most powerful engine."

The comment immediately attracted attention because the FIA's ADUO process was introduced specifically to monitor the competitiveness of manufacturers and identify whether any power unit supplier has gained a significant advantage.

Currently, the FIA assessments have not publicly established Mercedes as the outright benchmark, but instead identified Red Bull's co-produced with Ford engine as the most powerful, making Wolff's remark all the more noteworthy.

His comments prompted an immediate response from Red Bull's team principal Laurent Mekies, who urged the FIA to take the available data seriously before the current assessment window closes after Hungary.

According to Mekies, the governing body should ensure that any competitive imbalance is identified early enough to act if necessary, rather than waiting until the regulations are already in force.

The exchange adds another layer to the increasingly heated debate surrounding Formula 1's future power units. Concerns over energy deployment, engine parity and possible FIA intervention have dominated discussions for months, and Wolff's candid assessment is likely to increase scrutiny on Mercedes' development programme.

Ferrari's innovative rear wing design introduced during testing in Bahrain - Image: Race Pictures

At the same time, another political battle is unfolding over Formula 1's flexible rear-wing designs. According to reports, Red Bull has urged the FIA to go further than targeting individual concepts if changes are introduced. Instead of banning only specific solutions, the Milton Keynes-based team is reportedly lobbying for a blanket prohibition on all rotating rear-wing designs.

The debate follows increasing attention surrounding the so-called "McMacarena" concept, with Ferrari and McLaren as the teams most closely associated with innovative rear-wing movement under load, while Red Bull has struggled with the concept.

GPblog previously analysed the technical principles behind these designs, explaining how carefully controlled wing rotation can reduce drag on straights while remaining within current regulations. That analysis also highlighted why any FIA intervention could have implications well beyond a single team. And how Red Bull's design has caused problems.

If the governing body were to outlaw every rotating rear-wing concept rather than focusing on one particular interpretation, the competitive picture could shift dramatically. Such a decision would affect multiple teams currently developing similar aerodynamic solutions, rather than targeting a single design philosophy.

That would also leave Red Bull in an unusual position. With rivals continuing to refine concepts that could offer performance gains, the team is reportedly seeking a regulatory solution that applies equally across the grid instead of allowing alternative interpretations to survive.

With the Hungarian Grand Prix approaching, Formula 1 faces important decisions on both technical regulations and competitive fairness. Between questions over Mercedes' true engine performance and the growing dispute over rear-wing legality, the FIA is once again under pressure to prove that its regulatory framework can keep pace with the sport's rapidly evolving technology.

title: Socialist-backed Michigan Senate hopeful calls American politics a 'disease' after professing love for US
description: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed praised America before arguing the nation's political system is a "disease" and calling for ICE to be abolished.
fullText:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday described America's political system as a "disease" moments after professing his love for the country where he was raised.

El-Sayed delivered blistering attacks on the American political system during the final stop of "The People v. The Powerful" tour at DeVos Performance Hall in Grand Rapids.

He spoke at the event alongside Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as the trio criticized President Donald Trump, party leaders, corporations and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The Egyptian American physician and former public health official first reflected on the opportunities he said America had afforded him, noting he received an "incredible" public university education and a medical education funded through the National Institutes of Health.

Dem Senate Hopeful Abdul El-sayed Recounts Smashing Vodka Bottle After Beard Criticism

"No, don't get it twisted. I love America. I know exactly what America gave to me. I know what my life would have been, but for America," El-Sayed said. "I know what America can do, and at the same time, it's impossible not to reflect on the worst moments of those 250 years as well."

He then argued that Trump was merely a symptom of broader problems in American politics.

"Donald Trump is not, himself, the disease of our politics. He's just the worst symptom of the disease of our politics," El-Sayed said.

"The disease? It's the system that allows corporations and billionaires and special interests like AIPAC to buy and sell politicians to rig the system against us."

Ocasio-Cortez also echoed that message moments prior, telling the crowd, "You deserve a politics that treats the disease and not the symptoms."

Bill Maher Calls Out Bernie Sanders, Says He's Tired Of Hearing The Rich Don't Pay Their Fair Share Of Taxes

El-Sayed then targeted the nation's healthcare system, arguing that medical debt should be eliminated and contrasting its cost with federal spending on political campaigns and foreign aid.

"Medical debt shouldn't exist," he said, claiming the country's roughly $225 billion in medical debt could be erased for about $2.25 billion because it can be purchased "for a penny on the dollar."

He later turned his attention to ICE, calling it a "rogue agency" that should not exist.

"ICE has nothing to do with immigration. ICE has nothing to do with the southern border. ICE is about normalizing paramilitary forces on our streets. ICE is about weaponizing the idea of immigration against the Constitution itself. ICE cannot be reformed. ICE cannot be retrained. ICE has to be abolished."

The Senate hopeful also described himself as "dangerous" to a range of political and corporate interests, including health insurers and Democratic leaders.

"If you're Blue Cross Blue Shield, I'm dangerous," he said. "If you're Chuck Schumer, trading politicians like trading cards, I'm dangerous."
